questions.stem: A plant plans to introduce a two-part coating next month. Before selecting instruments or respirators, what should the hygienist do first?
options: Review the process, materials, tasks, quantities, exposure routes, and foreseeable upset conditions.
Begin production, monitor symptoms and odor complaints for several shifts, and then decide whether formal assessment is warranted.
Purchase the highest-protection respirator available and use it for every coating task.
Collect one area sample in the corridor without reviewing the coating operation.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Industrial hygiene begins with anticipation and recognition. Process and material information define what could be released, who may be exposed, and what evaluation strategy is appropriate before controls are selected.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Symptoms may be delayed, nonspecific, or absent; waiting defeats a preventive assessment.
Respirator selection requires contaminant, concentration, task, and atmosphere information, and PPE is not the first control by default.
A sample without a defined exposure question or representative location may not characterize worker exposure.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 8, anticipation, recognition, evaluation, and control, pp. 273-275

questions.stem: A blender operator moves between charging, mixing, and bagging stations during the shift. Which setup best estimates the operator’s inhalation exposure?
options: Use a stationary sampler above the production-room doorway and apply its result to every task performed during the shift.
Use a personal sampler with its inlet in the operator’s breathing zone during representative work.
A sample collected at the outdoor exhaust discharge.
A settled-dust sample collected from the control-room desk.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Personal sampling follows the worker and places the collection inlet near the nose and mouth, so it can represent the changing tasks and locations that contribute to inhalation exposure.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A doorway sample characterizes that location, not the operator’s changing breathing-zone exposure.
An exhaust-stack sample evaluates emissions or system performance, not personal exposure.
Settled dust in a remote area does not quantify airborne breathing-zone exposure during the tasks.

questions.stem: Opening a process valve can release a solvent vapor plume for less than one minute. The assessment objective is to determine the concentration during that brief event. Which approach is most suitable?
options: Use a single eight-hour integrated sample and interpret the shift average as the one-minute release peak.
Collect settled material from the floor after the shift.
Use a responsive direct-reading instrument or a validated short-duration grab-sampling method.
Place an unopened passive badge near the valve and read it immediately.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A brief release requires a method capable of resolving the short time interval. A full-shift integrated result may dilute the peak and fail to answer the stated question.
incorrectOptionExplanations: An integrated sample averages exposure over time and may not resolve a short peak.
Settled material does not measure the airborne vapor concentration during the release.
A passive sampler requires exposure over a documented period and laboratory analysis; an unopened badge collects no sample.

questions.stem: The objective is to measure airborne metal particulate generated by grinding. Which collection media is generally the most appropriate starting choice, subject to the selected analytical method?
options: A charcoal sorbent tube selected for organic vapors.
A whole-air bag used without a particulate collection medium.
A passive organic-vapor badge worn without confirming the analyte method.
A method-specified filter cassette attached to a calibrated sampling pump.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Filters are commonly used to collect airborne particulate, including many metal aerosols. The exact filter type, flow rate, and sample volume must follow the analytical method.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Sorbent tubes are generally used for gases and vapors and are not the normal collection medium for metal particulate.
A bag is generally used for grab samples of gases or vapors, not gravimetric or elemental particulate collection.
A vapor badge does not ordinarily collect the grinding particulate of interest.

questions.stem: A full-shift personal sample is needed for an organic solvent vapor. Which sampling train is most defensible?
options: Use the method-specified sorbent tube on a calibrated low-flow pump with the inlet in the breathing zone.
Use a cyclone and PVC filter because any airborne contaminant can be collected effectively on particulate media.
A high-volume area pump positioned outside the worker’s work area.
A bulk liquid sample substituted for airborne exposure monitoring.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Solid sorbent tubes are commonly used for organic vapors. The specific method determines sorbent, flow, duration, orientation, and maximum volume to avoid breakthrough.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A cyclone-filter train is intended for a particle-size fraction, not normally for collecting an organic vapor.
A remote area sample may not represent the worker’s personal exposure.
A bulk sample identifies material composition but does not quantify the worker’s airborne dose.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section II, Chapter 1 — Personal Sampling for Air Contaminants; NIOSH Manual of Analytical Methods (NMAM), Fifth Edition

questions.stem: A hygienist must evaluate the respirable fraction of dust generated during concrete finishing. Which configuration best addresses that objective?
options: Use a total-dust filter cassette on a nearby shelf and treat the stationary result as the worker’s respirable exposure.
Use the method-specified cyclone and filter at the required flow rate in the worker’s breathing zone.
A settle plate left beside the task until the end of the shift.
A sorbent tube operated at any convenient flow rate.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A cyclone separates much of the larger particle fraction so the downstream filter represents the respirable aerosol convention. Flow rate and sampler geometry are method-specific and affect the size cut.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A stationary total-dust sample does not necessarily represent personal respirable exposure.
Settling collection does not provide a quantitative respirable airborne concentration.
Sorbent tubes collect gases or vapors, and arbitrary flow changes can invalidate a method.

questions.stem: What feature distinguishes a passive vapor sampler from a pumped personal sampler?
options: It provides a continuous electronic concentration display without laboratory analysis.
It uses a high-volume pump to pull workplace air continuously through a particulate filter.
The contaminant reaches the medium by diffusion or permeation without a sampling pump.
It captures a single instantaneous volume in a sealed bag.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Passive samplers use a physical transport process rather than an active pump. Exposure time and the sampler’s validated uptake characteristics are needed to calculate concentration.
incorrectOptionExplanations: That describes a direct-reading instrument, not a typical passive badge.
A pumped filter system is active sampling.
That describes a whole-air grab sample.

questions.concept: Calibration with the complete sampling train
questions.stem: A technician calibrates a personal pump with open tubing, then attaches a high-resistance sorbent tube for sampling. What is the main data-quality concern?
options: There is no concern because a nominal pump setting remains accurate under every sampler resistance and battery condition.
Only the laboratory instrument requires calibration; field pumps do not.
The problem can be corrected by estimating flow from the tube color after sampling.
The sampling flow may change because calibration omitted the sampler’s representative resistance.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Sampler resistance affects pump flow. Calibration should be performed with representative media and connections in line, followed by post-sampling verification according to the method.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Pump performance can change with sampler resistance, battery condition, and other factors.
Accurate sampled volume depends on a calibrated field flow rate.
Tube appearance does not provide a traceable volumetric flow measurement.

questions.stem: A sampling pump reads 1.98 L/min before sampling and 2.02 L/min after sampling. The sample ran for 360 minutes. Using the average flow, what air volume was collected?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Average flow = (1.98 + 2.02) / 2 = 2.00 L/min. Volume = 2.00 L/min × 360 min = 720 L, or 0.720 m³.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This uses 1.00 L/min instead of the calculated average flow.
This adds the two flow readings and multiplies without dividing by two.
This introduces an incorrect factor-of-100 conversion.

questions.stem: A laboratory reports 0.54 mg of contaminant on a sample collected from 360 L of air. What is the airborne concentration?
options: 1.50 mg/m³
194 mg/m³
1,500 mg/m³
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Convert 360 L to 0.360 m³. Concentration = 0.54 mg / 0.360 m³ = 1.50 mg/m³.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This fails to convert liters to cubic meters correctly.
This multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing mass by air volume.
This applies the liters-to-cubic-meters factor in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: An analytical method has a limit of quantification of 0.004 mg per sample. The target airborne concentration is 1.6 mg/m³. What minimum air volume is required?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Vmin = LOQ × 1,000 / target concentration = 0.004 mg × 1,000 L/m³ ÷ 1.6 mg/m³ = 2.5 L.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This omits the cubic-meter-to-liter conversion factor.
This reverses the concentration and LOQ relationship.
This multiplies the two values rather than dividing LOQ by target concentration.

questions.concept: Interpreting a nondetect above the decision limit
questions.stem: A laboratory reports a result as less than 0.20 mg/m³, but the occupational limit used for the assessment is 0.05 mg/m³. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The exposure should be treated as zero because the laboratory did not report a concentration above its reporting limit.
The exposure is compliant because 0.20 mg/m³ was not measured.
Replace the occupational limit with the reporting limit because the analytical method defines the compliance criterion.
The result cannot demonstrate exposure below 0.05 mg/m³; use a more sensitive method or larger sample volume.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: “Less than 0.20 mg/m³” means the concentration was not quantified above that reporting threshold. Because the threshold is higher than the decision limit, compliance below 0.05 mg/m³ has not been demonstrated.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A nondetect is not proof that no contaminant was present.
The reporting limit is too high to resolve whether the result is above or below 0.05 mg/m³.
The analytical method must support the exposure decision; the decision criterion is not redefined by inadequate sensitivity.
